Whereas the Parliament of India has set out to provide a practical regime of right to 
information for citizens to secure access to information under the control of public authorities, 
in order to promote transparency and accountability in the working of every public authority, 
and whereas the attached publication of the Bureau of Indian Standards is of particular interest 
to the public, particularly disadvantaged communities and those engaged in the pursuit of 
education and knowledge, the attached public safety standard is made available to promote the 
timely dissemination of this information in an accurate manner to the public.

GLOSSARY OF AERONAUTICAL TERMS 

PART II MOTION OF AIRCRAFT 



0. Foreword 

9.1 Provides standard definitions of technical terms peculiar to aeronautics, astronautics and related 
subjects. Terms in general use in other branches of engineering are also included where they have 
some special relevance to aeronautics or astronautics. 

0.2 This standard consists of a series of parts, each part covering terms specific to a particular feature, 
type of aircraft, equipment, service, etc. 

0.3 The general arrangement of the terms is alphabetical. However, in certain cases related terms have 
been given together under a heading or general definition, and these are printed in distinctive italic type. 

0.4 Each term has been assigned a 4-digit or 5-digit number. The first one ( or two ) digit, in the 
thousandth place, represents the part number. This part number with the following digit in the 
hundredth place represents the section. The last two digits represent the position of the definition 
within a section. Thus the term 3405 is the 5th definition of Section 34, which is in Part III. 

0.8 Where two or more synonymous terms are in use, the term which is favoured is given first, with the 
intention that it should gradually displace the others. The alternative terms are given below the 
preferred terms in less prominent type. 

0.8 An Indian Standard Glossary of space terms covering definitions pertaining to rockets, missiles, etc, 
is also under preparation. 

0.7 Assistance has been derived from BS 185 'Aeronautical and astronautical terms' issued by the 
British Standards Institution in the preparation of this series of Indian standards. 



1. Scope — This part covers the standard definitions for terms relating to motion of aircraft. 

2. Terminology

the horizontal. 

The act of launching an object from the Earth's surface.

which has a component of velocity along the normal

Abbreviation for 'let-assisted take-off. 

Flight in which the aircraft is supported primarily by vertical

The tendency of an aircraft to pitch nose down in flight. 

Angular motion about the transverse axis.

2117 V/STOL Operations 



Definition 
Abbreviation for 'rocket-assisted take-off 9 . 

Angular motion about the longitudinal axis. 

Motion of an aircraft, relative to the ambient undisturbed air, 
which has a component of velocity along the transverse 
axis. 

A yawing' oscillation, the amplitude of which remains 
approximately constant. 

The tendency of an aircraft to pitch nose up in flight. 

Rearward motion of an aircraft along its longitudinal axis 
from a vertical, or near vertical, stalled attitude. 

Abbreviations as given below are used for the various modes 
of take-off ( TO ) and landing ( L ) of V/STOL aircraft: 
C for conventional. The required lift is derived from 
forward speed alone. 

S for short. The ground run is reduced substantially by 
powered lift or other means. 

V for vertical. Powered lift alone is used with no 

intentional ground run. 
RV for rolling. Essentially vertical but with a slow 

forward speed to ayoid ingestion of hot gases or 

debris. 

These letters are placed at the beginning with TO and/or 
Ladded thus:

STOL 


CTOL 


RVTOL 


VTO 


STO 


CTO 


RVTO 


VL 


SL

RVL

SECTION 22— MOTION IN FLIGHT 

Manoeuvres intentionally performed with aircraft, other than 
those required for normal flight ( see 2215 ). 

To cause the transverse axis of arr aircraft to take up an angle 
to the horizontal. 

A manoeuvre in which an aircraft performs part of an inverted 
loop. 

Of a V/STOL aircraft. The ect of making any necessary ad- 
justments to effect transition. 

A steep descent, with or without power. 

A dive during which en aircraft reaches its terminal velocity. 

An aerobatic manoeuvre in which aeroplane rolls from side to 
side while still facing in the same direction. 

The change in flight path between the approach and the 
landing. 

To travel horizontally after flare-out and before lending. 

A gradual descent with little or no thrust. 

A benked continuous gilding turn. 

Of e heavier-than-air aircraft. To remain epproximetely 
stationary in relation to the ground or to the air mess. 
Sometimes called position hover when releted to ths 
ground. 

A closed flight path of en aeroplane in a vertical plane. 
Normally the dorsal surfaces remain on the inside of the 
curved flight path.

Definition 

A loop in which the dorsal surfaces remain on the outside 
of the curved flight path. 

All flight regimes necessary for travel from point to point, 
that is taking-off, climbing, straight and level flight, 
descending, turning, side-slipping and landing provided 
it does not entail abrupt variations in height or in atti- 
tude of the aircraft ( see 2201 ). 

a) To land beyond the intended area ( see 2237 ). 

b) To break off a final approach. 

Recovery from a dive. 

The process of returning to substantially straight and level 
flight from a manoeuvre. 

A partial or complete rotation of an aircraft about its longi- 
tudinal axis. 

A lateral oscillation of an aircraft, particularly one in which 
the ratio of the rolling to yawing motion is appreciable. 

A rapidly executed roll in which autorotation of the wing 
may be used to speed up the manoeuvre. 

A half loop followed by a half roll with the aeroplane flying 
in the opposite direction. 

A continuous spiral descent in which the mean angle of 
incidence exceeds the angle of stall. 

A spin at a large mean angle of incidence, with the longi- 
tudinal axis more nearly horizontal than vertical. 

A spin in which the aircraft is inverted and the wing incidence 
exceeds the negative stalling incidence. 

A spin in which sustained oscillations are present, the most 
marked being in roll and pitch, for example, the rate of 
roll changes from zero to a high value and back again in 
each cycle. 

A height of 15 metres used for determination of take-off 
distance. For low speed aircraft a screen height of 1 1 
metres also is in common use. 

Speed at which the steady climb is initiated and maintained. 
It is equal to or higher than the unstick speed. 

Speed at which the pilot pulls the control column back, so 
that the aircraft starts rotating in order to get airborne. 

Speed at which the aircraft gets airborne. 

a) To bring an aircraft into the flight condition in which the 
wings are stalled. 

b) To heve reached such a condition. 

The ect of flying an aircraft to the condition at which it stalls. 

A manoeuvre in which an aircraft is pulled up into a steep 
climb until about to stall, when one wing is allowed to 
drop and the aircraft falls into a dive. 

a) Of a V/STOL aircraft Passage from hovering to flight 
in which the aircraft is mainly supported by the aero- 
dynamic lift derived from forward motion, or vice versa. 

b) Of a supersonic aircraft. Passage from subsonic to 
supersonic flight or vice versa. 

c) This is the phase between the point where the eircraft 
just leaves the ground and the point where it sets into 
a steady climb to achieve a height of 16 metres.
